analysis.one_liner: Requires two-person crews, more wheel-bearing detectors, bigger fines, and faster tank car upgrades on hazardous-material trains.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill with bipartisan support in December 2023 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never held a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the months after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio derailment, this bill would tighten federal safety rules for trains carrying hazardous materials. It would require at least two crew members on large freight trains, mandate networks of detectors that catch overheated wheel bearings before they cause derailments, speed up the retirement of older tank cars, raise fines for safety violations, and give first responders advance information about what hazardous cargoes are coming through their communities. It would also charge each large railroad $1 million a year to fund local hazmat training and let workers take the time they need for safety inspections. The bill cleared committee on a bipartisan basis but never came up for a vote on the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live along freight rail routes, especially in towns like East Palestine where a derailment can release toxic chemicals; rail workers, who get a two-person crew floor and protection of inspection time; and local firefighters and emergency planners, who get advance cargo information, a funded training program, and direct access to train consist records during an emergency. Drivers and pedestrians also gain from new requirements on blocked railroad crossings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail-side communities, rail workers, first responders

how_it_helps.text: Requires Class I freight trains to operate with at least a two-person crew (a certified conductor and a certified engineer), with exceptions that do not apply to high-hazard trains or trains 7,500 feet or longer.

Requires large railroads to build and maintain defect detection systems, including wheel-bearing (hotbox) detectors spaced so trains are scanned roughly every 10 to 20 route miles depending on the technology used, and to act on alerts before derailments happen.

Speeds up the phase-out of older DOT-111 tank cars carrying flammable liquids, generally by December 31, 2027, several years earlier than existing deadlines, with a possible one-year delay if manufacturing capacity falls short.
Raises maximum civil penalties for rail safety violations to as much as $1 million per violation, and up to $5 million for violations causing death, serious injury, or imminent hazard.

Requires large railroads to generate accurate real-time electronic train consist information, share it with emergency-response fusion centers, and provide commodity flow reports to state and tribal emergency response commissions, and bars withholding consist information from first responders during an incident.
Imposes a $1 million annual fee on each Class I rail carrier to fund local hazardous-materials emergency response training grants, and doubles the cap on supplemental training grants to $4 million.

Bars railroads from limiting the time an employee needs to complete a railcar, locomotive, or brake inspection, and directs audits of whether inspection programs give inspectors adequate time and whether managers pressure employees to sign off on inspections.
Requires every railroad to maintain a toll-free telephone number for the public to report blocked highway-rail grade crossings, a problem that traps residents and delays emergency vehicles.

analysis.who_pays: The large Class I freight railroads (Union Pacific, BNSF, CSX, Norfolk Southern and similar carriers), which would bear the cost of crew staffing, detector networks, inspection staffing, the annual $1 million fee, and larger potential fines. Tank car owners would bear retrofit and replacement costs, and railroads would likely pass some compliance costs to shippers through freight rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Class I freight railroads and their shippers

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs fall on the railroads, and freight railroads would likely pass a share of them to shippers through rates, which can eventually show up in consumer prices; the bill does not offset those costs.

Owners of older tank cars must retrofit or replace them by December 31, 2027, and the bill allows the Transportation Secretary to push the deadline back a year if manufacturing capacity is insufficient or commerce would be significantly affected, so the fleet transition carries real cost and some schedule risk.

The committee-reported version is softer than the bill as introduced: the crew requirement now applies only to Class I railroads and grandfathers existing one-person operations unless the Secretary finds them unsafe, and the introduced flat mandate for a hotbox detector on every 10-mile segment was replaced with risk-based detector plans that railroads can satisfy with approved alternatives.

Many of the bill's core obligations are delivered through future Transportation Department rulemakings on timelines of one to two years, so the actual stringency would depend on how the agency writes the rules rather than on the statute alone.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted at a real, demonstrated risk: catastrophic derailments of hazardous-material trains in populated areas, a risk the country saw vividly in 2023. The costs are real but fall on a small number of very large, highly profitable carriers, and the strongest honest objection is rate pass-through to shippers plus the fact that much of the mandate is delegated to rulemaking. The trade-off favors the bill; the serious weakness is the version reported by committee, which diluted some of the introduced bill's mandates.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor business in December 2023, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 1, 2023 by Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio together with a bipartisan group of co-introducers including Senators Vance, Casey, Rubio, Fetterman, Hawley, Smith, Klobuchar, Braun, Romney, Marshall, and Baldwin.
It had 11 cosponsors, six Republicans and five Democrats.
The Senate Banking Committee held hearings on it in March 2023, and the Senate Commerce Committee ordered it reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute in May 2023.

On December 13, 2023, the Commerce Committee, chaired by Senator Cantwell, reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 284.
No further action appears in the record: the bill sat on the Senate calendar and never received a floor vote or Senate passage before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large Class I freight railroads came out ahead: they avoided the bill's two-person crew requirement, defect detector mandates, faster tank car phase-out, $1 million annual fee, inspection protections, and sharply higher fines, all without ever having to defeat it on a recorded vote.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio and lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Railway Safety Act of 2023 in the Senate and recruited a bipartisan group of co-introducers.

for.name: J.D. Vance
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio and original co-sponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its most prominent Republican co-sponsor, giving it bipartisan cover from a state marked by the year's most serious rail disaster.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment and moved it onto the Senate Legislative Calendar in December 2023.

for.name: Bipartisan cosponsor bloc (6 Republicans, 5 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Republicans Rubio, Hawley, Braun, Romney, and Marshall, keeping the bill bipartisan from introduction through committee approval.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the committee-approved bill for a Senate floor vote during the remainder of the 118th Congress, leaving it on the calendar until the term expired.

against.name: Association of American Railroads
against.role: Trade group for the major freight railroads
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed central provisions such as the two-person crew requirement and pressed to soften or defeat the bill, in one of the most heavily lobbied rail-safety fights in years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at every recorded step: an Ohio Democrat and an Ohio Republican introduced it together, its 11 cosponsors split 6 Republican and 5 Democrat, and a Democratic-led committee approved it; the obstruction it met came from the floor-scheduling stage, not from a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed two-person crews, defect detector networks, minimum inspection time, a $1 million annual fee, real-time cargo disclosure to first responders, and fines up to $1 million to $5 million per violation. By dying without a vote, the railroads kept all of these costs and mandates off their books.

A faster phase-out of DOT-111 cars would force owners to retrofit or replace older cars by the end of 2027, a cost to lessors and shippers, but it also guarantees builders a wave of mandated replacement and retrofit demand. The public benefit is a safer fleet; the industry split between who pays and who earns.

The bill guarantees two-person crews on large trains, bars railroads from limiting inspection time, and directs audits of whether managers pressure workers to sign off on inspections, all long-standing union priorities. With the bill dead, existing one-person and rushed-inspection practices continue.

industries.industry: Rail shippers (chemical, agricultural, and other freight customers)
industries.note: Shippers benefit from safer, more reliable service and fewer blocked crossings, but railroads would likely pass some compliance costs through freight rates. The bill's death preserves current rate structures along with current risk.
